From 5 people in a small Bucharest apartment to building one of the world’s leading automation companies. To anyone doubting themselves, may this story inspire you!

Daniel Dines grew up in Romania and taught himself how to code.

He moved to the US and landed a job at Microsoft, with a stable salary, stock options, and health insurance. For an immigrant, that can feel like the dream.

Then he quit and moved back to Bucharest to start his own company.

𝐇𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞.
↳ UiPath started with 5 people in a small apartment in Bucharest
 ↳ It took 10 years to raise its first seed round
 ↳ In 2018, it became Romania’s first unicorn
 ↳ In 2021, it listed on the New York Stock Exchange

But one part of Daniel’s story stood out to me: the culture he built.

Early on, he asked his team what allowed 10 engineers from a small country to keep some of the largest enterprises in the world happy.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲.

Humility became UiPath’s 1rst company value, and the rest grew from there. Today, its 4 values are Humble, Bold, Immersed, and Fast.

Daniel has said that growing up under communism taught him to distrust marketing narratives. Instead, UiPath focused on building great software and trusting customers to recognize its value.

Today, UiPath has grown to more than 3,000 people around the world and is expanding beyond automation into business orchestration, where AI agents, robots, and people work together within governed processes.

Quite a journey from 5 people in a Bucharest apartment. 

P.S. P.S. Let me know if youd like to see the full 15-minute interview.

Can enterprise AI scale without sacrificing trust?

At
UiPath
FUSION, I spoke with
Andrada Morar
, VP of Customer Experience and Global Partnerships, to explore what it takes to coordinate agents, deterministic automation, systems, and people without losing accountability, context, or trust.

One idea stayed with me:
“Deterministic where you can, agentic where you can’t, humans where you must.” This goes beyond technology architecture. It calls for leadership discipline.

We discussed why process authority must come before automation, how co-innovation with partners is reshaping enterprise AI, why governance must extend across every decision and exception, and why human judgment should remain an intentional design principle.

The conversation also surfaced a more useful way to think about AI. Not as artificial intelligence replacing people, but as individual augmentation that expands what people can accomplish while keeping authority clear.

Watch our conversation and read my full take on
UiPath
’s vision for end-to-end enterprise orchestration at FUSION:

We need to talk about governance. Whether you’re looking to get a grip on agent sprawl in your business or starting to build up your agentic program.

What I heard an AI leader share at
UiPath
FUSION: “Are your agents working safely, accurately, ethically, and are they auditable? Start with the 100th agent in mind! If you start when the 20th agent is in production, you’ll be writing an incident report.” Ouch!

Another point I kept hearing several times from customers: build a “kill-switch” into your agents to stop a runaway agent in the future. Ensure you have a way to roll back an agent’s code to a previous, working state. This approach ensures you don’t put the company at risk of runaway actions or cost, and non-performance.

But when it comes to governance, ensure you agree within the team on the expected return and if the goal is worth pursuing. Help educate the organization on what AI and agents can do realistically and cost-effectively to ground the expectations.

Finally, different levels of impact carry increasing levels of risk (team-, org-, or company-level). Establish agent registries and review processes before agents go live to address it early.

How have you set up your agentic AI governance process?

As a teenage swimmer, I wanted an Olympic gold medal.

Yesterday in Bucharest I shared a stage with someone who won one.

David Popovici joined
Raluca Negulescu-Balaci
of the
UiPath Foundation
and me on day one of
Impact SEE
to talk about excellence. David described having to come to terms with being too hard on himself, which let us ask whether harshness is an enemy of excellence. Most high-performance cultures I've worked in assume the opposite.

Raluca talked about building excellence in kids who've been handed fewer chances than most. The Foundation stays with them from around age 10 through the end of secondary school, and I was proud to celebrate that work there.

As an American, I get Europe as a single story. "The EU" is growing, or "The EU" is stalling.

IMPACT brings together leaders from business, technology, politics, science, and culture, and day one gave me the regional version from people running companies and governments across South Eastern Europe.

Poland is outgrowing nearly every major economy in the EU, while Romania is putting one of the bloc's largest shares of GDP into investment.

I work for a company founded in this city, and I still showed up with the one-story version in my head.

Also, I made the Romanian evening news. More precisely, David made the evening news. I was in the shot.

For the last year, enterprise AI has been obsessed with taking humans out of the loop.
UiPath
made the opposite case: build better systems for humans and AI agents to work together.

But there’s a missing layer needed to make that collaboration work: context.

UiPath announced its approach:

🗺️ 𝗠𝗮𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸
A living, governed definition of how work actually happens, including processes, rules, exceptions, systems, and human judgment.
🧭 𝗨𝗶𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗲𝗿
Builds and maintains that Map from knowledge spread across documents, systems, and people, while humans approve what becomes part of it.
📚 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲𝗿
Captures decisions and exceptions as work happens, so new knowledge can be proposed back into the Map instead of getting lost.
🛤️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀
Turn approved context into execution while keeping agents and workflows within defined boundaries.

The bigger shift is that context stops being something an agent simply retrieves at runtime and becomes part of the operating system of work itself.

The future of work isn’t just about giving agents more intelligence. 

It’s about giving humans and agents the shared context they need to work well together.

A CIO with hundreds of bots already running doesn't want to hear "rip and replace." So what do you tell them about AI agents? I put that question to
Vikram Kakumani
, Deputy CTO at
UiPath
, at FUSION 2026 on
The Ravit Show
.

This one got deep into architecture:
- How to take an RPA estate with hundreds of bots into agentic automation
- What "controlled agency" really means, and where humans should stay in the loop
- The biggest blocker keeping AI agents out of production
- Orchestrating agents, robots and people together
- The architecture mistake companies keep making with agents
- How the Map of Work gives agents the enterprise context they're missing
- Where Maestro takes orchestration next

The part that stuck with me was controlled agency. Everyone wants agents that act on their own. Very few teams have decided where a person still needs to sign off. Vikram laid out a practical way to draw that line.

Where would you keep a human in the loop for your agents?
